items.prompt: What does the acronym 'SOLID' stand for?
choices: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation, Dependency inversion
Structured, Optimized, Logical, Independent, Documented
Simple, Object-oriented, Lightweight, Interchangeable, Durable
Scalable, Ordered, Layered, Isolated, Deployed
items.explanation: SOLID is an acronym for five specific design principles, each addressing a different way a codebase can become hard to change.
items.reference:
SOLID
S O L I D
5 principles, 5 different failure modes
Why: this unit focuses on the D, the one most responsible for L1's scenario.

items.prompt: According to L1, which SOLID principle is most directly responsible for the 12-file ripple in the scenario?
choices: Dependency inversion
Single responsibility
Liskov substitution
Interface segregation
items.explanation: The scenario's root cause — high-level code directly constructing a concrete low-level class — is exactly what the dependency inversion principle addresses.
items.reference:
SOLID
S O L I D
5 principles, 5 different failure modes
Why: this unit focuses on the D, the one most responsible for L1's scenario.

items.prompt: What does the 'dependency inversion principle' say?
choices: High-level code should depend on an abstraction, not a specific concrete implementation, which should be handed in from outside
Every class should depend on as many other classes as possible for maximum reuse
Dependencies should always be listed in reverse alphabetical order
A class should never depend on any other class under any circumstances
items.explanation: DIP is specifically about depending on an abstraction rather than a concrete implementation, with the concrete choice injected from outside rather than constructed internally.
items.reference:
Dependency inversion
🧩 Depend on the abstraction
📥 Concrete choice injected from outside
Why: this is what breaks the ripple from a single vendor decision.

items.prompt: In L1, what does each of the 12 classes do that violates dependency inversion?
choices: Each one constructs `SendgridEmailClient` directly and internally, rather than receiving an email-sending abstraction from outside
Each one avoids using any email-sending functionality at all
Each one imports 12 different unrelated libraries
Each one is missing proper error handling for network failures
items.explanation: Each class hardcodes the concrete `SendgridEmailClient` internally, exactly the pattern DIP identifies as the problem.
items.reference:
Dependency inversion
🧩 Depend on the abstraction
📥 Concrete choice injected from outside
Why: this is what breaks the ripple from a single vendor decision.

items.prompt: What is an 'abstraction,' as this unit defines it?
choices: A description of what something does, without committing to how, that multiple different implementations can satisfy
A class that has no methods or properties at all
Any piece of code that's difficult to understand
A concrete class that's been renamed to sound more general
items.explanation: An abstraction is a contract about behavior ('can send a message') that many different concrete classes can implement, without specifying the mechanism.
items.reference:
Abstraction
❓ What, not how
🔀 Multiple implementations can satisfy it
Why: depending on the 'what' is what makes swapping the 'how' cheap.

items.prompt: In L1, what is the abstraction that both Sendgrid and Postmark clients could satisfy?
choices: Something with a method that can send a message, regardless of the underlying vendor
A specific class named exactly 'SendgridEmailClient'
A configuration file listing API keys
A shared database table storing sent emails
items.explanation: The abstraction is the shape of 'can send a message' — any class with a matching method satisfies it, regardless of which vendor it wraps.
items.reference:
Abstraction
❓ What, not how
🔀 Multiple implementations can satisfy it
Why: depending on the 'what' is what makes swapping the 'how' cheap.

items.prompt: What is 'dependency injection'?
choices: The practical mechanism for DIP: a dependency is passed into a class from outside, rather than the class constructing it internally
Automatically installing missing npm packages when code runs
A testing technique that deliberately introduces bugs to check test coverage
Storing configuration values in environment variables
items.explanation: Dependency injection is specifically the mechanical technique that implements DIP — passing a dependency in, usually via a constructor, instead of constructing it internally.
items.reference:
Dependency injection
📥 Passed in, not built internally
🏗️ Usually via the constructor
Why: this is how DIP actually gets implemented in real code.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what does the 'single responsibility' principle say?

The five, briefly

L: safe substitution
I: no unused-method dependencies

items.prompt: According to L2, does DIP mean every class should always depend on an interface, even for things that will never have a second implementation?
choices: No — DIP is about places where the concrete choice is genuinely likely to vary or where testability specifically requires a fake
Yes — every single dependency in a codebase should go through an interface
Yes, but only for classes with more than 100 lines of code
No, because interfaces are a deprecated feature in modern languages
items.explanation: L2 explicitly scopes DIP to places where variation or testability genuinely matters, not as a blanket rule for every dependency in a codebase.
items.reference:
Not everywhere
🎯 Apply where variation is real
🚫 Don't apply where it never will vary
Why: over-applying DIP adds indirection with no real payoff.

items.reference:

items.prompt: Implement `OrderService`, matching L3's fixed version: its constructor should accept an `emailClient` and store it; `placeOrder(order)` should call `this.emailClient.send(order.customerEmail, 'Order confirmed', \`Order ${order.id} confirmed\`)` and return the result. The class must not construct any concrete email client itself.

tests.description: sends via the injected client with the right recipient and subject
tests.expr: (() => { class FakeClient { send(to, subject, body) { return { to, subject, body }; } } const svc = new OrderService(new FakeClient()); const result = svc.placeOrder({ id: 5, customerEmail: 'x@y.com' }); expect(result.to).toBe('x@y.com'); return expect(result.subject).toBe('Order confirmed'); })()

tests.description: the body includes the order id
tests.expr: (() => { class FakeClient { send(to, subject, body) { return { to, subject, body }; } } const svc = new OrderService(new FakeClient()); const result = svc.placeOrder({ id: 9, customerEmail: 'z@z.com' }); return expect(result.body).toBe('Order 9 confirmed'); })()

tests.description: works with any client implementing send(), tracked via a spy
tests.expr: (() => { class SpyClient { constructor() { this.calls = []; } send(to, subject, body) { this.calls.push({ to, subject, body }); return { sent: true }; } } const spy = new SpyClient(); const svc = new OrderService(spy); svc.placeOrder({ id: 9, customerEmail: 'z@z.com' }); expect(spy.calls.length).toBe(1); return expect(spy.calls[0].body).toBe('Order 9 confirmed'); })()

items.explanation: OrderService never mentions a specific vendor — it only assumes whatever it's given satisfies the 'has a send() method' abstraction, which is exactly what let L3 swap Sendgrid, Postmark, and a fake client in with zero changes to this class.
items.reference:
Zero lines changed
✅ Sendgrid, Postmark, Fake — same OrderService code

items.prompt: Implement `NotificationService`, applying the same dependency-inversion pattern as `OrderService` to a different domain: its constructor should accept a `channel` and store it; `notify(userId, message)` should call `this.channel.send(userId, message)` and return the result.

tests.description: calls send on the injected channel with the right arguments
tests.expr: (() => { class FakeChannel { constructor() { this.sent = []; } send(userId, message) { this.sent.push({ userId, message }); return { ok: true }; } } const ch = new FakeChannel(); const svc = new NotificationService(ch); svc.notify(42, 'hello'); return expect(ch.sent).toEqual([{ userId: 42, message: 'hello' }]); })()

Zero lines changed
